proved.label: Proved
proved.means: Checked by the Lean proof assistant, with no gaps. Click a name to read the proof.

measured.label: Measured
measured.means: Approximate on real trades, so we measure it instead of proving it: see VALIDATION.md.

choice.label: Our choice
choice.means: A rule we picked to stay careful. Not maths, and we say why.

unchecked.label: Can't check
unchecked.means: Something I cannot see or know. I tell you what to do about it.

steps.title: I turn your trades into one number: the evidence
steps.flip: First I ask: if this were pure luck, how surprised should I be?
steps.plain: I weigh your trades against every possible size of edge at once, small to large, and average the results. That gives one number, the evidence. With no edge it averages exactly 1, so the bigger it gets, the less luck can explain it.
steps.formula:
e = average over edge sizes λ ≥ 0 of  exp(λS − λ²n/2)
  = (2/√v) · exp(ρ²S²/2v) · Φ(ρS/√v),   where v = 1 + ρ²n
steps.formula_note: S is your total divided by the spread of your trades, n the number of trades, and the edge sizes λ are weighted by a half-normal curve of width ρ.

claims.text: The formula in the code is exactly this average.
With no edge the evidence averages exactly 1; with a losing edge, at most 1.
claims.assumes: Normal trades with a known spread.

claims.text: More profit always means more evidence, never less.

Real trades are not perfectly normal, and their spread has to be estimated. So we test it: on 42,000 made-up strategies with no edge, it called one a real edge 0.15% of the time, and at most 1.9% in the hardest case.

steps.title: I say “real” only past a bar of 40
steps.flip: Luck would need a 1-in-40 fluke to fool me. Same for “losing”.
steps.plain: Because the evidence averages 1 when there is no edge, it rarely climbs to 40 by luck. Calling “real edge” at 40 on one side and “losing” at 40 on the other leaves at most a 5% chance of a false call in total. That is the 95% in the range you see.

claims.text: The range and the verdict are the same statement: “real edge” exactly when the whole 95% range is above zero.
The code's search for the range's ends always finds the right point.
Evidence that averages at most 1 reaches 40 at most 1 time in 40 (Markov's inequality).
When your total is positive, the “losing” side can't pass at the same time.

steps.title: Every version you tried raises the bar
steps.flip: Tried 40 settings and kept the best? Then I need 40 times more evidence.
steps.plain: Try enough versions of a strategy and one will look great by luck alone. So every version you tried and every strategy you show me count as one family, and the bar grows with the family. Versions you tried but didn't show count as zero evidence.
steps.formula: one strategy, N versions:   real edge  ⟺  e ≥ 40 · N

claims.text: Across any number of strategies and versions, false “real edge” calls stay under 5% of all such calls on average, however the strategies relate to each other (the e-BH procedure).
The code's procedure is exactly that one, whatever order ties come in, and a version you didn't show is never selected.
For one strategy and N versions the rule is simply: real edge exactly when the evidence reaches 40 × N.
Keeping the best of N versions and dividing its evidence by N is still fair evidence.
Keep the best of 1,000 random versions without saying so and I'm fooled 51% of the time. Say you tried 1,000 and it falls to 0.2%. That's why I ask.

steps.title: Checking again and again doesn't fool me
steps.flip: Look after every trade if you like. I was built for that.
steps.plain: An ordinary 95% range checked after every trade is wrong about half the time, because sooner or later luck pokes out of it. Mine holds at every check at once: under luck the evidence behaves like a fair game that can't drift up, and such a game rarely ever reaches 40.
steps.formula: P(the evidence ever reaches 40, at any number of trades) ≤ 1/40      (Ville's inequality)

claims.text: Ville's inequality: a fair or losing game that starts at 1 ever reaches 40 at most 1 time in 40.
Under luck, the evidence is such a game.
So the 95% range holds at every number of trades at once, and a strategy with no edge, or a losing one, is ever called real at most 1 time in 40.
claims.assumes: Independent normal trades with a known spread.

claims.text: With the spread estimated from your trades and a check every 10 trades: wrongly “real” 0.5% of the time for ordinary trades, 1.9% for streaky ones.
No range before 30 trades. A spread measured on a handful of trades is too unsteady to promise anything (see my mistakes below).

steps.title: Lopsided and streaky trades get a higher bar
steps.flip: Many small wins and a rare huge loss fool simple tests. So I get stricter, never looser.
steps.plain: When losses are rarer but bigger than wins, a few dozen trades can look great before the big loss arrives. When trades move together, they carry less information than their count suggests. In both cases I raise the bar.

claims.text: The lopsidedness adjustment can only raise the bar and widen the range, never the opposite.
The streakiness factor never narrows the range: it stays between 1 and 10.
Its main ingredient is right: when trades follow each other like an AR(1) process, the spread of the average grows by (1 + r)/(1 − r) as trades pile up.
What the guards buy, measured: martingale-like records were called real 37% of the time at 30 trades before them, now 0%; lopsided ones 3.4%, now under 1%.
Nothing is called real before five losing trades: an unseen loss could be any size.

steps.title: Everything around the verdict adds up
steps.flip: The coin flips, the streak odds, the money sentence and the paired trades are checked too.
steps.plain: Around the verdict sit smaller calculations: the coin-flip picture, the odds of a losing streak, the money sentence, the live-vs-backtest range, the drawdown, the time in the market and the pairing of exchange fills into trades. Where they are exact, they are proved; where they are estimates, they say so.

claims.text: “Your average trade is up but you lost money: your losing trades were bigger” is said only when it is a theorem, when every trade's percent and money point the same way. Otherwise I point at fees and costs.
The live-vs-backtest range adds a 97.5% range on each side, so it holds at 95% even when you check your live trades often.
The range on your win rate is Wilson's: exactly the rates a fair test wouldn't reject.
My own forecasts are graded with the Brier score, which rewards honest probabilities, and compared with always guessing the usual rate, not just with a coin flip.
The losing-streak odds are exact: the code's calculation equals the probability over every possible sequence of wins and losses.
The coin-flip picture is a fair test: if your trades were pure luck (symmetric around zero), a result this good would show up no more often than the picture says.
The page draws 1,000 random flips, not all of them, so its count carries a little noise. And it is only a picture: the verdict comes from the evidence.
Pairing an exchange's buys and sells first in, first out keeps every coin and every dollar accounted for.
The worst drop and the trades since your peak are computed exactly as defined.
Time in the market is the true length of the union of your trades' time spans.
The drawdown odds, “faded” and the live-vs-backtest odds come from resampling your own trades: estimates, and labelled as such.

limits.text: Real trades are not normal, their spread is estimated, and they can depend on each other. The proofs above assume the textbook case; for real trades I measure instead. That is where 0.15%, and 1.9% at worst, come from.

I can't see your code. A backtest that peeks at future prices or skips fees hands me trades that look better than they were. When the shape looks too good, I flag it and give you a prompt to have the code checked.
The past is not the future. A real edge can stop working, which is why I check whether it has faded, and why you should come back.
When the evidence decides fastest is a rule of thumb: tuned for about 100 trades, though the exact best is near 112. It costs 0.03%.

mistakes.title: I showed a range from just two trades.
mistakes.impact: At 2 trades it missed the true average 9% of the time, against the 5% I promise; for someone checking after every trade from 2 on, about 13%.
mistakes.found: The Lean proof assumes a known spread, so a test checked what happens with an estimated one.
mistakes.fix: No range before 30 trades, where verdicts start. From there it holds (about 2.2%).

mistakes.title: My coin-flip sentence could contradict my verdict.
mistakes.impact: A passing card could read “3 copies ended higher … a pass needs 1 or fewer … It passes.” The picture and the verdict are different tests.
mistakes.found: A test checking the coin-flip proof's conditions against 400 random records.
mistakes.fix: The bar is now said as odds, never as a count of copies. The verdict itself was never affected.

mistakes.title: I blamed trade sizes when fees were the cause.
mistakes.impact: “Your losing trades were bigger” was said even when every trade was up in percent and down in money, which happens when fees are in the money but not in the percent.
mistakes.found: Proving the sentence showed exactly when it is true.
mistakes.fix: It is said only when it is a theorem. Otherwise I say the percent and the money point opposite ways, and why.

mistakes.title: One blank cell broke my money sentence.
mistakes.impact: A single empty percent cell turned the average into “n/a”, and could invent a mismatch between percent and money, or hide a real one.
mistakes.found: A test checking the money sentence against its theorem.
mistakes.fix: Only trades with both numbers count now.

mistakes.title: My report card set the bar too low.
mistakes.impact: I called my own forecasts “better than guessing” when they beat a coin flip. But always guessing the usual rate beats a coin flip too.
mistakes.found: Proving what the Brier score rewards.
mistakes.fix: I now compare my forecasts with always guessing the usual rate.

mistakes.title: A rounding tolerance misread large amounts.
mistakes.impact: A strategy exactly back at its high could read “0.000000 USDT below your peak, 2 trades ago”.
mistakes.found: A test comparing the drawdown with its definition.
mistakes.fix: The tolerance is now relative to the size of the numbers.

mistakes.title: A shortcut far below zero.
mistakes.impact: Where the evidence is tiny, a one-term shortcut overstated it by up to 1.5%. It never changed a verdict.
mistakes.found: A test comparing the code with the proved formula.
mistakes.fix: The exact formula is used there now.

mistakes.title: I said my tuning was the best at 100 trades.
mistakes.impact: It is best near 112 trades; at 100 the difference is 0.03%.
mistakes.found: Trying to prove the claim showed it is only approximately true.
mistakes.fix: Worded as the rule of thumb it is.

mistakes.title: Three kinds of records fooled me in testing.
mistakes.impact: Lopsided records were wrongly called real 3.4% of the time, martingale-like ones 37% at 30 trades, streaky ones checked often 3.4%.
mistakes.found: The validation run on records whose truth is known.
mistakes.fix: A higher bar for lopsided trades, five losses before “real”, and a streakiness floor. Now under 1%, 0% and 1.9%.
